vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: The money that you pay every month to live in a place
Money or things that you give to help other people
Relaxed: you feel good and calm in a place
A person who takes care of a sick person, often someone in the family
To start to feel at home in a new place
A person who works without pay to help other people
A part of a city where people live

paras: In March, the board approved a small pilot: three apartments near the hospital. They are for families who come from other states for long cancer treatments. Each apartment has two bedrooms and a living room where the family can eat together.

Ana is the nurse who talks to every family before they arrive. "Many of our patients come from cities that are very far from Sao Paulo," she says. "The rent here is very high for them, so they used to stay in cheap hotels where they felt lonely."

Lucia is a mother from Belem who stayed in the first apartment with her son, Pedro. Pedro is twelve, and he has leukemia. "The neighborhood is quiet, and there is a small park where Pedro can play," she says. "Our neighbors were volunteers who helped us with everything."

The pilot also gets donations. A supermarket which is two blocks away sends food every week, and a group of caregivers that met at the hospital organizes a dinner every Friday. "In the first week, we were nervous," says Lucia, "but we settled in fast. It was the first place in Sao Paulo where we felt comfortable."
reading.source: A short story written for this lesson, based on the housing pilot that Fernando planned in Lesson 25.

listenings.text: Hi, everyone. My name is Carlos, and I am one of the volunteers who help the families in the housing pilot. I am retired, and I live in the building where the three apartments are. Every Monday, I meet the new families at the hospital and walk with them to the apartment. I show them the supermarket which sends the food, the pharmacy that is open all night, and the small park where the children play. Many families are very tired when they arrive. Some of them traveled for two days by bus. For me, the most important thing is simple: on the first night, nobody in our building eats dinner alone.

Hi Fernando, it's Sarah. I read the newsletter article that you sent me, and I loved it. The story about Lucia and Pedro is exactly the kind of story which the board in Texas wants to hear. I have two questions for our next call. First, how many families were able to use the apartments in the first two months? And second, who is the person that organizes the volunteers? In Texas, we have a social worker who does that, and it makes a big difference. Oh, and one more thing: can you send me a photo of the living room where the families eat together? Talk soon!
